newsitem.title: USA: Toys "R" Us goes on trial for holding prices high.
newsitem.headline: Toys "R" Us goes on trial for holding prices high.

text.p: Barbie dolls and other playthings cost more than they should at Toys "R" Us, the government will argue at a trial Wednesday, alleging the nation's largest toy seller illegally stifles competition.

Lawyers for Toys "R" Us readily concede the toy dealer has higher prices than some of its competitors. But they plan to argue vigorously that the toy retailer's executives have every legal right to cajole manufacturers into restricting sales to warehouse club retailers like Price Club, which cuts prices aggressively.
"Toys "R" Us' conduct in this case is supported by 100 percent" of the legal precedents, said Michael Feldberg, the toy company's lawyer. "It's not even close."

Federal Trade Commission lawyers plan to assert Toys "R" Us throws its weight around -- it has about one-fifth of the American toy market -- to stop the competition, in violation of the Federal Trade Commission law.

"The facts show that what they did was use their market clout to obtain agreements to cut off the clubs from a supply of popular toys," said Mark Whitener, deputy director of the FTC Bureau of Competition.

The trial before Administrative Law Judge James Timony starts Wednesday and will last weeks. Unlike some of the abstruse issues that come before the FTC, this is not merely a fight about the law. Toys "R" Us and the government don't even agree about what happened.
Essentially, the FTC argument is this:

Toys "R" Us felt price pressure from warehouse clubs on popular toys like Mattel's Barbie. Making matters worse, the deals undercut the toy store chain's low-price image in ads with the slogan: "Lower prices. Bigger selection. Guaranteed."

To forestall direct price comparisons, the government alleges, Toys "R" Us orchestrated understandings with toy makers -- and between toy makers -- to sell the warehouse clubs only "combo packs" costing more than open stock.
Consumers could not make direct price comparisons when they found Barbie packaged with Ken or extra outfits.

The lead lawyer for Toys "R" Us said the government has it all wrong. He said the toy store chain was faced with the problem of warehouse clubs which picked and sold only the hottest items of the season, riding free on the advertising of Toys "R" Us and other legitimate retailers.
Toys "R" Us argues it merely let the toy makers know that it "reserved the right not to carry identical items sold by the manufacturer to warehouse clubs."
This policy "is clearly protected, indeed endorsed, by all relevant precedent," the company argues. Beyond that, Toys "R" Us argues that it lacks power to control the market.
"Wal-Mart, not Toys "R" Us, generally leads prices down," argues the toy retailer in papers filed with the FTC.
The FTC agrees that Wal-Mart undercuts Toys "R" Us prices, but says warehouse club prices were even lower.

If the administrative law judge finds for the government he will issue a "cease and desist" order against Toys "R" Us, but no monetary damages. The toy company would face money damages if it failed to follow the order.
Whichever side wins, the result is appealable to the full, five-member FTC and then to a federal court of appeals.
Toys "R" Us' stock edged up 37.5 cents to $27.375 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
